To set a default currency in People Analytics and add exchange rates for converting from your default currency to another, you need to select a default currency in portal.
Doing so will enable you to choose a default currency for displaying your payroll information. This is particularly useful if your PeopleXD solution processes payroll in both the UK (£) and Ireland (€).
Note: By default, the solution’s currency is set to GBP
Default solution currency
To set a default currency, follow the steps below in portal.
From the dashboard menu, select People Management.
Click Data Centre.
Beside People Analytics Configuration, click Open.
Click the Currency tab.
From the Select Default Currency drop-down menu, select a default currency.
Click Save.
Add Currency rates
The solution employs a process called constant currency when converting values to a single currency. It uses only one exchange rate per currency for calculations, regardless of how many periods are involved. The exchange rates are based on the last day of the selected period in the Time picker.

for calculations, regardless of how many periods are involved. The exchange rates are based on the last day of the selected period in the Time picker. The constant currency method effectively analyses cost changes over time. If varying exchange rates were applied, differences in values could arise from the fluctuations, which would not be visible in the analysis as they occur before display. By using constant currency, trends in costs and trend line slopes are represented through a consistent exchange factor, offering a clearer and more reliable view of cost changes between periods.
To add currency rates, follow the steps below in portal.
From the dashboard menu, select People Management.
Click Data Centre.
Beside People Analytics Configuration, click Open.
Click the Currency tab then click Add Exchange Rate.

Configure Pay Planner to apply proration to bonus calculations and ensure employees receive a bonus that reflects their actual contribution period. Two proration methods are available.
📌Note: You need Pay Planner admin access to configure proration.
Start-date proration: Which you configure in the incentive plan settings.
Custom factor proration: Lets you upload individual factors per employee during cycle set-up.
Start-date proration
Start-date proration adjusts an employee's bonus based on how long they have been employed during the bonus period. When you enable this, Pay Planner automatically calculates a proration factor for any employee who did not work the full bonus period, and reduces their bonus proportionally. To turn on start-date proration, follow the steps below.
From the dashboard menu, select Pay Planner.
Click Settings, then click Incentive Plans.
Click the pencil icon to edit the relevant bonus plan.
Select the Employment start date checkbox, then click Save.
📌 Note: This setting applies to all employees in any cycle that uses this bonus plan. Employees who worked the full bonus period are unaffected.
Custom factor proration

ng applies to all employees in any cycle that uses this bonus plan. Employees who worked the full bonus period are unaffected.
Custom factor proration Custom factor proration lets you upload a proration factor for each affected employee, and gives you flexibility to handle scenarios that start-date proration cannot accommodate — such as leave of absence or partial-year arrangements. The factor is a decimal between 0 and 1 and is displayed as a percentage in Pay Planner.
You can upload the file during the Bonus step of the New Cycle wizard, or in the set-up stage under Budget. To upload custom proration factors, follow the steps below.
⚠️Warning: Once the cycle moves to the allocation stage, you cannot upload, remove, or replace the file.
During cycle creation, go to the Bonus step.
Alternatively, in the Set-up stage, go to the Budget tab, click Bonus, then click Edit.
Under Upload individual proration, click Upload file.
🤓Tip: Use the Download template link to get the correct file format. The file must be saved as a CSV file and contain two columns: Employee ID and Factor.
Click Save.

wnload template link to get the correct file format. The file must be saved as a CSV file and contain two columns: Employee ID and Factor.
Click Save. ⚠️Important: Uploading a new file replaces the previous file and does not merge with it. Employees not included revert to a 100% factor. For example, if you upload employee A and employee B at 0.75, then upload a file with only employee A at 0.5, employee A updates to 50% and employee B loses their custom factor.
📌Note: You cannot update individual employee factors directly on the screen. To make any change, reload the complete file with all required factors included.
How the two methods interact
If both start-date proration and a custom factor are active for the same employee, both apply and multiply together to produce the final factor that the system uses in the bonus calculation. For example, if start-date proration produces a factor of 0.8 and the employee also has a custom factor of 0.75, the effective proration is 0.6 (0.8 × 0.75).
If an employee has no custom factor uploaded, the system assumes a factor of 100% and only start-date proration applies if you enable it. If a custom factor is uploaded but start-date proration is not enabled, only the custom factor applies.

Bonus plans define how to calculate bonuses in your compensation cycles. Set up your bonus plan formula once in Pay Planner settings. It applies when you create a cycle that includes bonus as a pay type. You need Pay Planner admin access to do this.
Available bonus formulas
Pay Planner supports five standard bonus formulas. Each formula applies selected performance factors as multipliers against the budgeted bonus. Employees receive their full bonus only when all performance targets are met.
📌 Note: If your formula includes team performance, you must set team performance targets when you create a compensation cycle. Apply a single percentage across all teams, or adjust each team individually.
Budgeted bonus × company performance × individual performance.
Budgeted bonus × (company performance × company weight + individual performance × individual weight).
Budgeted bonus × (company performance × company weight + team performance × team weight) × individual performance.
Budgeted bonus × company performance × (team performance × team weight + individual performance × individual weight).
Budgeted bonus × company performance × team performance × individual performance.
Configure a bonus plan
To set up your bonus plan formula, follow the steps below. Changes to your bonus plan apply to new cycles only. Existing cycles are not affected.
From the dashboard menu, select Pay Planner.

When creating your compensation cycle in the setup stage, you can select how manager budgets are calculated. There are two options to select from:
Budget Method
Description
Uniform Budgeting

the setup stage, you can select how manager budgets are calculated. There are two options to select from:
Budget Method
Description
Uniform Budgeting Is where each manager's budget is based only on employee base pay. For example, if a manager has two employees, one earning £50K and the other £100K, and the merit increase is 10%, the budget would be £15,000.
This method doesn't take performance or recommendations into account, meaning managers may end up over or under-budget based on actual recommendations.
Flexible Budgeting
Uses your pay philosophy recommendations to calculate each manager's budget. For example, a team of high performers may be allocated a larger share of the budget.
It's a more dynamic approach, but requires careful management to stay aligned with overall strategy.

Username accounts allow employees to access PeopleXD Evo when a verifiable email address isn't available. However, email accounts are strongly recommended as best practice for authentication, security policy compliance, and self-service account management.
Active employees with email addresses on PeopleXD automatically sync to Access Evo Members. If an employee doesn't have an email address on their record, they don't sync automatically.
To set up a username account, an administrator must sync the account manually, set a temporary password, and email the login details to the user.
Username account limitations
Username accounts have the following limitations:
Users cannot manage their own password resets: Access Evo administrators must set temporary passwords for account creation or when a user forgets their password. This creates additional administrative overhead for IT teams.
Cannot apply company security policies: Security policies manage user authentication and session management, and are defined based on email domains. If a user doesn't log in with an email address, only the Default Security Policy in Access Identity can be applied.

Organisation-Level MFA allows organisations in Access Evo to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) requirements on their users, independently of and in addition to the existing domain security policy.
This means each organisation can set its own minimum authentication requirement that applies specifically to its users, regardless of whether the domain itself enforces MFA. The Organisation Administrator configures this in the Security Options page within Organisation Settings.
Getting started
Prerequisites
Before configuring Organisation-Level MFA, ensure you have Organisation Administrator access in Access Evo.
Accessing the security options page
The Organisation-Level MFA setting is found in Organisation Settings in Evo.
Sign in to Access Evo as an Organisation Administrator.
Go to Organisation Settings, then open the Security Options page.
The Minimum Authentication Requirement control appears here.
📌Note: The Security Options page is only visible to Organisation Administrators. Standard users and managers do not have access to this setting.
Authentication levels
The Minimum Authentication Requirement determines which sign-in methods users must satisfy. There are four levels, ranging from password-only to phishing-resistant hardware authentication.

Security considerations
Each authentication method carries different security risks. Access Evo displays these risks in the Security Options UI to help you choose the right level for your organisation.
Method

Can be intercepted via SIM-swapping attacks and is vulnerable to phishing.
Authenticator app (TOTP)

FIDO2 hardware key
Phishing-resistant and cryptographically secure — the recommended option for high-security environments.
Configure Organisation-Level MFA
Set the Minimum Authentication Requirement
To set the Minimum Authentication Requirement, follow the steps below.
Go to Organisation Settings then in Access Evo, click Security Options.
Locate the Minimum Authentication Requirement setting.
Select the level appropriate for your organisation.
Save your changes.
📌Note: Changing this setting takes effect immediately. Users who do not have a qualifying MFA method already configured will be redirected to set one up on their next sign-in.

For example, if your organisation requires SMS (Level 1) but the domain policy has SMS disabled, users will not be able to satisfy the requirement.

User sign-in experience
When a user signs in to Evo and your organisation has an MFA level configured, Evo follows this process:
The user signs in with their email address and password.
Evo checks whether the user's organisation has an MFA level configured.

The user signs in with their email address and password.
Evo checks whether the user's organisation has an MFA level configured. If the user already has a qualifying MFA method set up and enabled, Evo prompts them to verify using that method and they can proceed.
If the user does not have a qualifying MFA method, Evo redirects them to Access Identity to set up the required MFA method.
📌Note: Evo only redirects users to set up MFA if their existing method does not satisfy the configured level. Users who already have a higher-level method are not affected.

Members sync automatically creates and maintains Access Evo user accounts for your employees. When you set up a new employee in PeopleXD, their Access Evo member record is created automatically. When an employee leaves, their Access Evo account is deactivated based on your leaver rules.
How members sync works
PeopleXD is the source of truth for your employee records. Members sync transfers employee data from PeopleXD to Access Evo in one direction only. Changes made to member records in Access Evo don't sync back to PeopleXD.
How this supports other Access Evo applications
When you connect other applications to Access Evo, employees already exist as users. You don't need to set up and invite users again to the system. You just need to update their access to provide permissions to the other applications.
When an employee leaves, their record is automatically deactivated on Access Evo. This removes the risk of forgetting to revoke access for other applications they can access through Access Evo.
What data is synced
Members sync transfers these data points from PeopleXD employee records to Access Evo member records:
Email
Forename
Surname
Reports to manager
Job title
Department
Location
Status
You can't change which data points are synced. The list is pre-defined and not configurable.
When data is synced
Members sync runs at different frequencies depending on the type of update.

This guide covers how to query the PeopleXD (CoreHR) database using Oracle SQL Developer. All access is read-only — you cannot change, delete, or break any data in PeopleXD. This is a safe environment to learn and experiment.
SQL Dialects — Important
There are different types of SQL. At Oxford HR Systems, we use two:
Oracle PL/SQL — used in SQL Developer to query the PeopleXD database directly. This is what this guide covers.
TSQL (Transact-SQL) — used in Visual Studio when editing .RDL report files. Broadly similar to Oracle SQL but has syntax differences. If you copy SQL from one environment to the other, it may need adjustments.
When searching online for SQL help, always specify which dialect you are using (e.g. search "Oracle SQL GROUP BY" not just "SQL GROUP BY"). MySQL, PostgreSQL and other dialects also exist but are not used in this role.
Connecting to the Database
When you open SQL Developer you will see a list of saved connections on the left-hand panel. Each connection represents a different database or environment (e.g. UOXZ for the Z environment). Once you have connected to a database, any query window you open will run against that database. The connection name is shown at the top of each query window so you always know which environment you are querying.

en will run against that database. The connection name is shown at the top of each query window so you always know which environment you are querying. The database objects panel (left side) shows Tables, Views, and Functions available to your connection. The HR data we work with is owned by the core HR user, which owns the BI layer — the views we query sit within this schema.
Always use Views, not Tables
By agreement with the Access Group, HR Systems queries data from views rather than tables directly. Views are pre-built by the Access Group and give you clean, reliable fields. You will see tables listed in SQL Developer but you should not query these directly unless you have a specific reason and are confident in what you are doing.
Common views you will encounter:
PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER — person-level data including forename, surname, person reference, pay group, employment status.
Appointment history views — appointment-level data including appointment ID, start dates, status.
Functions also exist in the database (Oracle built-in functions and custom Access Group functions). These are used for things like pulling UDF (User Defined Field) information and salary data. You will encounter them when reading existing SQL scripts. They appear as function names followed by brackets containing parameters.
Basic SELECT Statement
The simplest SQL query selects data from a view or table.

Basic SELECT Statement
The simplest SQL query selects data from a view or table. Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM view_name
Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
This returns every person's forename and surname from the entire database. Separate column names with commas. You can select as many columns as you need.
Using a WHERE Clause
A WHERE clause filters the results. Add it after the FROM clause.
Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM view_name WHERE condition
Example — filter to active employees only:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER WHERE employment_status = 'S'
Employment status 'S' means active (commenced) in PeopleXD. Most queries should include this filter to exclude dormant and historical records.
WHERE Clause Operators
You can use a range of operators in WHERE clauses:
= (equals) — exact match. String values need single quotes; numeric values do not.
Example: WHERE forename = 'Sarah'
!= or <> (not equals) — excludes a specific value.
Example: WHERE employment_status != 'S'
> < >= <= — greater than, less than, etc. Useful for dates and numbers.
IN() — matches any value in a list. String values need single quotes; numeric values do not.
Example: WHERE pay_group IN (10, 20, 30)
Example: WHERE surname IN ('Smith', 'Jones')

Example: WHERE pay_code NOT IN (100, 105)
BETWEEN — matches values within a range (inclusive). Good for dates and numbers.
Example: WHERE start_date BETWEEN '01-JAN-2025' AND '31-DEC-2025'
LIKE — pattern matching using wildcards. Requires single quotes.
% at the start means ends with: WHERE surname LIKE '%ton' (returns Preston, Morton, Thurston etc.)
% at the end means starts with: WHERE surname LIKE 'Smi%'
% at both ends means contains: WHERE view_name LIKE '%pay%calendar%'
NOT LIKE — opposite of LIKE.
IS NULL — finds records with no value in that field.
IS NOT NULL — finds records that do have a value.
Combining Conditions
Use AND, OR, and NOT to combine multiple WHERE conditions.
Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
AND surname LIKE '%ton'
If you have a syntax error (pink wiggly underline in SQL Developer), check that you have used AND, OR, or NOT between each condition. Missing an operator is one of the most common errors.
ORDER BY
Add ORDER BY at the end of your query to sort results.
Syntax:
SELECT column1 FROM view_name ORDER BY column1
Default sort is ascending (A to Z, 0 to highest). To sort descending, add DESC:

o sort results.
Syntax:
SELECT column1 FROM view_name ORDER BY column1
Default sort is ascending (A to Z, 0 to highest). To sort descending, add DESC: ORDER BY surname DESC
Column Aliasing
You can rename columns in your results using AS (the alias keyword). This is useful when column names are long or when you are using aggregation functions.
Example:
SELECT COUNT(person_reference) AS number_of_people FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
You can also omit AS and just put the alias name after the column — Oracle accepts both:
SELECT COUNT(person_reference) number_of_people FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
Note: do not use reserved words like GROUP as an alias — Oracle will reject it.
Commenting Out Code
Two dashes (--) comment out everything after them on that line. The query engine ignores commented text.
Uses:
1. Soft-delete a line without removing it — useful when testing different versions of a query.
2. Add explanatory notes to your SQL that other people can read.
Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S' -- active employees only
-- AND pay_group = 10 -- temporarily removed for testing
Aggregation and GROUP BY
Aggregation functions perform calculations across multiple rows. The most common ones are:
COUNT() — counts the number of rows.
SUM() — adds up numeric values.
MAX() — returns the highest value.
MIN() — returns the lowest value.

MIN() — returns the lowest value. When you use an aggregation function, every other column in your SELECT must appear in a GROUP BY clause. GROUP BY goes after the WHERE clause.
Example — count people by pay group:
SELECT pay_group, COUNT(person_reference) AS headcount
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
GROUP BY pay_group
ORDER BY pay_group
HAVING Clause
HAVING filters results after aggregation has been applied, whereas WHERE filters before aggregation. HAVING goes after GROUP BY.
Example — only show pay groups with more than 50 active employees:
SELECT pay_group, COUNT(person_reference) AS headcount
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
GROUP BY pay_group
HAVING COUNT(person_reference) > 50
JOINs
Joins combine data from two or more tables or views. Modern syntax uses JOIN in the FROM section rather than the old-style plus signs in the WHERE clause (you may see the old syntax in legacy SQL — do not write it, but be aware it exists).
The three main join types used in HR Systems:
INNER JOIN — returns only rows where there is a match in both tables. Rows with no match are dropped from both sides.
Example:
SELECT pm.forename, pm.surname, ah.appointment_id
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER pm

both tables. Rows with no match are dropped from both sides.
Example:
SELECT pm.forename, pm.surname, ah.appointment_id
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER pm INNER JOIN appointment_history ah ON pm.person_reference = ah.person_reference
WHERE pm.employment_status = 'S'
LEFT JOIN — returns all rows from the first (left) table, and matched rows from the second table where they exist. Where there is no match, the second table columns return NULL. This is the most commonly used join type in HR reporting, for example joining to diversity data where not every person has a diversity record.
FULL OUTER JOIN — returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible and returning NULLs where there is no match on either side.
When joining tables, prefix column names with the table or view name (or its alias) followed by a dot, to avoid ambiguity:
pm.person_reference (person_reference from PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER aliased as pm)
ah.person_reference (person_reference from appointment_history aliased as ah)
You can add extra conditions to a JOIN clause using AND:
INNER JOIN appointment_history ah ON pm.person_reference = ah.person_reference
AND ah.employment_appointment_status = 'commenced'
Chaining multiple JOINs can cause rows to multiply if the joined table has multiple matching records. Be careful and check row counts as you build complex queries.

Exporting Results Once your query returns results:
1. Right-click on the results grid.
2. Select Export.
3. Choose CSV format — this is the most reliable option.
4. Do not use INSERT format (this exports as SQL code for importing into another database).
5. Do not use the Excel export — it can miss rows depending on what is highlighted.
6. Browse for a save location, click Next, then Finish.
Debugging Tips
Pink wiggly underline in the editor — syntax error. Hover over it to see the error message. Click the pink bar on the far right of the screen to jump to the error line in a long script.
Toggle line numbers — right-click the script pane and select Toggle Line Numbers. Essential when an error message refers to a specific line number.
Soft-delete with comments — use -- to comment out suspect lines rather than deleting them, so you can restore them easily if needed.
Column count error in GROUP BY — if Oracle says a column is not in the GROUP BY clause, check that every non-aggregated column in your SELECT is listed in the GROUP BY.

HOW TO — Add a Pay Code to the HR Report Suite SQL
Background
The HR Report Suite contains a set of .RDL (Report Definition Language) files that define the HR reports available to users. Each .RDL file includes an embedded dataset called DataSet1, which contains the main SQL query that drives the report.
Within DataSet1, the SQL includes a hard-coded IN() list of numeric pay codes. This list controls which pay codes are included in the report output. When a new pay code is created in PeopleXD, it will not appear in the HR Report Suite output until it is manually added to this list in each affected .RDL file.
This is a TSQL change (not Oracle PL/SQL). The files are edited in Visual Studio 2017, accessed via CONNECT Remote Services.
Affected report files are typically those in the allowances suite, including PERDEP01 Full Data Set, PERDEP01 Full Data Set with Allowances, and PERDEP20 Approved Allowance Changes, though other files may also be affected depending on the pay code type.
All files in a report suite are versioned together. If you update one file you must increment all files in the suite to the same version number.

HOW TO — Raise a Change Request for HR Reporting (OSM)
What is OSM?
OSM (Oxford Service Management) is the University of Oxford's IT change control system. Any change to HR Reporting infrastructure — including SQL changes, report file edits, and configuration changes — must be recorded and approved via an OSM Change Request (CR) before work begins. This ensures a full audit trail and supports the university's change management governance requirements.
For HR Systems reporting changes, the Change Request is raised in PeopleXD's OSM module and follows a 14-section format.
When Do You Need a CR?
A Change Request is required before:
- Any edit to SQL within a .RDL report file
- Any change to a shared dataset or data source
- Deployment of updated report files to the TEST or LIVE environment
- Any configuration change to the HR Reporting environment
Raising a CR is always the first step — before any files are opened or edited.
The 14-Section CR Format
All Oxford HR Systems Change Requests use the following section structure. A blank template is available in the hris-change-requests GitHub repository at templates/change-request-template.md.
Section 1 — Details: What is changing? Describe the specific change being made, the files or systems affected, and the environment pipeline (TEST then LIVE).

1 — Details: What is changing? Describe the specific change being made, the files or systems affected, and the environment pipeline (TEST then LIVE). Section 2 — Justification: Why is the change necessary? Describe the business reason, the problem being solved, and any deadlines or dependencies.
Section 3 — Related Changes: Are there any dependent changes that must happen at the same time or in a specific sequence? If none, state that explicitly.
Section 4 — Impact on Dependent Services: What is the impact on connected or downstream services? Who will be affected when the change is live?
Section 5 — Downtime: Will there be any service outage or at-risk period? If not, explain why not.
Section 6 — Effect of Not Applying: What happens if this change is not made? Describe the ongoing business impact of leaving the issue unresolved.
Section 7 — Risk Assessment: What could go wrong? How likely is it and how serious? What mitigations are in place?
Section 8 — Testing: Who will test the change and how? What criteria must be met before the change can be promoted to LIVE?
Section 9 — Implementation Plan: A numbered list of steps using the format: Step N — [action]. Owner: [name]. Each step should be on one line. Cover the end-to-end process from initial edit through to LIVE sign-off.

he format: Step N — [action]. Owner: [name]. Each step should be on one line. Cover the end-to-end process from initial edit through to LIVE sign-off. Section 10 — Communications Plan: Who needs to be informed and when? For minor internal reporting fixes, this is often minimal.
Section 11 — Business Owner / Approver: The person accountable for approving the change. For HR Systems reporting changes this is typically Marie Cooksey, Head of HR Systems.
Section 12 — Potential Security Impact: Does the change alter access controls, expose new data, or affect user permissions? Describe any security implications.
Section 13 — How Security Impact Will Be Tested: How will you confirm that no unintended access or data exposure has resulted from the change?
Section 14 — Back-Out Plan: A numbered list of steps to reverse the change if something goes wrong after deployment. Use the same Step N format as Section 9. Include an estimate of how long rollback will take and confirm whether rollback results in any data loss.
Key OSM Fields
When submitting the CR in OSM, two fields that are commonly confused:
Category — the type of item being changed. Common values: Report, Software, Data Fix, Configuration, Document, Enhancement, Patch. For changes to .RDL report files, use Report.

m being changed. Common values: Report, Software, Data Fix, Configuration, Document, Enhancement, Patch. For changes to .RDL report files, use Report. Justification / Type — the reason for the change. Common values: Bug Fix, Enhancement, Upgrade, Patch. For correcting a missing pay code or similar SQL omission, use Bug Fix.
These are separate fields. A typical HR reporting CR will have Category = Report and Justification = Bug Fix.
The Change ID
When OSM assigns a Change ID (the CR reference number), note it immediately. This number must be entered into the Report Summary comment block at the top of the DataSet1 SQL in each affected .RDL file. The format is:
-- Change ID: [OSM number]
This ensures every deployed report file is traceable back to its authorising Change Request.
CR Template and Completed CRs
The blank CR template is held in the hris-change-requests GitHub repository:
hris-change-requests/templates/change-request-template.md
Completed CRs are stored in:
hris-change-requests/CRs/
Naming convention for CR files: CR-YYYY-MM-DD-short-description.md (kebab-case, lowercase, date = date drafted).
Example: CR-2026-06-18-pay-code-121-hr-report-suite.md
Guidelines for Completing the CR
Never invent information. If you do not know a value, use [TBC] or mark it for confirmation.
Always confirm Section 11 (Business Owner / Approver) before finalising.
